subject: Art & Design
title: Color Blindness: Designing for All Eyes
description: A quick win: understand Color Blindness: Designing for All Eyes.

hook.text: Eight percent of men can't distinguish red from green. If your design relies on color alone, millions can't use it.

buildup.text: Color vision deficiency affects 300 million people worldwide. The most common type confuses red and green hues.

discovery.text: Accessible design uses redundant cues: icons, patterns, labels, and contrast — never color as the only differentiator.

twist.text: Traffic lights look identical to colorblind users. They navigate by position — top, middle, bottom — not by color.

climax.text: Facebook is blue because Mark Zuckerberg is red-green colorblind. Blue is the color he sees most vividly.

punchline.text: Good design doesn't just look right. It works for every eye.

quiz.question: Why should designers avoid using color as the only way to convey information?
options: Color vision deficiency affects millions, making color-only cues inaccessible

details.summary: Approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women have some form of color vision deficiency, most commonly red-green confusion (deuteranopia/protanopia). Designers must ensure information is never conveyed by color alone — adding labels, patterns.
details.whyItMatters: A chart using only red and green to distinguish data excludes nearly one in twelve male viewers. Color-accessible design isn't an edge case — it's designing for hundreds of millions of people and is often legally required by accessibility standards.
takeaways: About 8% of men have color vision deficiency
Never convey information by color alone
Approximately 300 million people worldwide are affected

faq.question: What is the most common type of color blindness?
faq.answer: Red-green deficiency, which includes deuteranomaly (reduced green sensitivity, about 5% of males) and protanomaly (reduced red sensitivity, about 1% of males). These make it difficult to distinguish reds from greens and certain oranges from yellows. Complete color blindness is extremely rare.

faq.question: How can designers test for color accessibility?
faq.answer: Use simulation tools like Sim Daltonism, Chrome's DevTools color blindness filters, or Stark plugin for Figma. Convert designs to grayscale to check if information is still clear. Follow WCAG contrast guidelines. Always pair color indicators with text labels, icons, or patterns.
